title: Why One Bad Bulb Can Turn Off All Your Christmas Lights
description:
Why can one bulb turn off a whole string of lights? Many light strings are wired in series: one single loop, and the power has to flow through every bulb in a row. Inside each bulb a thin wire glows. If it snaps, the loop is broken and every light goes dark.

That's why newer bulbs hide a tiny bypass called a shunt: when the wire burns out, the power jumps across it and the rest stay lit. But a loose or missing bulb still breaks the loop, so check for the loose one first and push it back in.

Have your lights ever gone dark like this? Tell us below.

More true whys: https://www.youtube.com/@truewhys?sub_confirmation=1

Sources: U.S. Department of Energy, "How Do Holiday Lights Work?"; Michigan State University Extension, "Why did my string of holiday lights go out?"; HowStuffWorks, "How Christmas Lights Work"; US patent 4,727,449 (filament bypass shunt).
